title: Union-Find: Count Connected Components
oneLiner: Instead of re-traversing the graph from scratch every time a new connection arrives, union-find merges two groups in almost constant time and remembers the merge forever.
keyTakeaway: A union-find (disjoint set) structure answers "are these two already connected?" and "merge these two groups" incrementally, edge by edge -- unlike a fresh BFS/DFS from every unvisited node, it never has to re-explore the whole graph when one more connection shows up, which is exactly what algorithms like Kruskal's MST need when edges arrive one at a time.
explanation:
A union-find structure starts with n separate singleton groups, tracked in a `parent` array where parent[i] = i for every i -- every node is its own group's root. Two operations: Find(x) walks parent pointers up from x until it reaches a node that's its own parent (the root of x's group); Union(a, b) finds both roots and, if they differ, makes one root point at the other -- merging the two groups into one.

Processing a list of edges is then just: for each edge (a, b), call Union(a, b). If Find(a) already equals Find(b), they're already in the same group -- nothing changes. If they differ, the merge reduces the total component count by exactly one. After every edge is processed, the number of distinct roots remaining IS the number of connected components.

Watch the parent array below: notice most entries stay unchanged for a long time -- a merge overwrites only one root's entry, and Find may also shorten the paths it walks; union-find only ever touches what a merge actually requires, not the whole structure.

recognitionSignals: The problem is about grouping items into connected sets based on pairwise connections (edges, "these two are the same group"), and asks how many groups exist, or whether two items end up in the same group.
You need to repeatedly ask "are these two already connected?" and "merge these two groups" as new connections arrive, without re-scanning everything each time.
gotchas: Skipping path compression (or union by rank/size) still gives a correct answer, but Find can degrade toward O(n) per call on a long chain -- fine for small inputs, worth knowing for anything performance-sensitive.
Forgetting to check Find(a) == Find(b) before unioning (and decrementing the component count) either double-counts a merge or corrupts the running count.
confusableWith: Graphs: BFS Traversal / DFS Traversal (Fundamentals track) can also answer "how many connected components," by running a traversal from every unvisited node -- union-find answers the same question incrementally, one edge at a time, which matters when edges arrive over time (like in Kruskal's MST algorithm) rather than being fully known up front.

complexity.note: Here V = n nodes and E = the number of edges. Setting up the parent and size arrays is O(V); then each of the E edges does two finds and at most one union. With path compression (halving here) AND union by size together, each of those is amortized inverse-Ackermann, α(V) -- effectively O(1) -- so the whole pass is O(V + E·α(V)), effectively O(V + E). (With only one of the two techniques, a find is amortized O(log V), giving O(V + E log V).) Space is the parent and size arrays.

referenceSolutions.python:
def count_components(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))
    size = [1] * n

    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path compression (halving)
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    components = n
    for a, b in edges:
        root_a, root_b = find(a), find(b)
        if root_a != root_b:
            if size[root_a] < size[root_b]:  # union by size: hang the smaller tree under the larger
                root_a, root_b = root_b, root_a
            parent[root_b] = root_a
            size[root_a] += size[root_b]
            components -= 1
    return components
